title: GKD-Recruiter: Jointly Modeling Social and Task Heterogeneity for Spatial Crowdsourcing via Graph Knowledge Distillation
one_liner: Pick whom to recruit for location-bound tasks by combining social spread, worker-task fit, and a search policy that avoids wasting recruits on already-filled tasks.
lead: Spatial crowdsourcing is not only about who hears about a task. It is also about who can physically reach the place, wants that kind of task, and still adds value after other workers have already covered the demand. This paper builds all three pieces into one system. It represents workers, tasks, and social links in one graph, turns that graph into scores for likely task completion, and then searches over recruitment choices so that extra recruits are not spent where the task is already full.

problem.h2: Why recruiting the most connected people is not enough
paras: A social recruitment system starts with a small seed set of workers and asks them to pass tasks through their contacts. That sounds close to classic influence maximization, where the goal is to trigger the largest spread. But spatial crowdsourcing adds two constraints that break that simple view. First, hearing about a task does not mean doing it, because a worker may be far away or may dislike that task type. Second, each task needs only a limited number of workers, so after the demand is met, more successful recruitment adds no value.

Those two constraints create a hard planning problem. You need to choose seeds whose contacts both receive the task and have a real chance to show up. You also need to avoid oversupplying one task while another stays empty, because wasted recruitment on a full task leaves fewer opportunities to fill the remaining ones.

callout.html: The paper maximizes effective task satisfaction, not raw message spread, because only workers who both receive the task and fit its place and type can finish useful work.

panels.title: 5. The system picks seeds with balance
panels.caption: It favors seed sets that spread well and fill more task slots, because both conditions are needed.

steps.text: Create a graph with worker nodes, task nodes, and social links so that the system can reason about both who knows whom and who fits which task.
Estimate how likely each worker is to do each task based on location and task type, because receiving the task alone is not enough.
Estimate how likely each worker is to recruit specific contacts so that the system can predict who may hear about the task next.
Combine task-fit and social-spread signals into one representation so that the planner sees both who can be reached and who can actually help.
Use a learned search policy to choose seeds while accounting for task saturation, because greedy additions can get stuck on already-full tasks.

paras: The paper changes the target object from social spread to effective task satisfaction. That means the system scores a recruitment plan by how many useful task slots it fills, not by how many workers merely receive the announcement.
object.object: effective task satisfaction under social recruitment

hidden.name: expected useful coverage of each task
paras: The hidden quantity is the expected useful coverage for each task: how many task slots are likely to be filled by workers who both hear about the task and can actually do it. This number matters because raw spread can look large even when the recruited workers are too far away or have no interest in that task type.

The system estimates useful coverage by combining two probabilities. One probability describes whether recruitment reaches a worker through social links. The other describes whether that worker is a good match for the task. The product is useful because a worker helps only when both events happen.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark worker-task pairings that are more likely to fill a still-useful slot.

reads.html: Useful coverage asks, for each task, how many needed worker spots are likely to be filled by people who both get the message and can really do the job.
The framework estimates expected task satisfaction from joint social diffusion and worker-task affinity, because only their overlap produces completed tasks.

paras: A planner that looks only at social spread will overvalue well-connected workers whose contacts cannot or will not perform the tasks. A planner that looks only at worker-task fit will miss the fact that good workers may never hear about the task. The joint graph fixes that gap because it lets the model trace both the communication path and the task-fit path at the same time.

The search stage matters because the reward is not nicely additive. Suppose one more recruit would likely help Task A, but Task A is already almost full. A greedy rule may still choose that recruit because the local score looks high. The learned search policy can avoid that trap by evaluating how the whole seed set changes remaining task demand, so that it spends seeds where they add new filled slots instead of duplicate coverage.

stages.s: more filled task slots with less oversupply

math.h2: A compact view of the objective
math.words: For each task, add up the workers who are expected to both receive the task and complete it, but stop counting once the task demand is filled.
math.equation: ETS = sum_t min(d_t, sum_w p_reach(w,t) * p_fit(w,t))
symbols: effective task satisfaction, the total useful filled demand across tasks
the demand of task t, meaning how many workers that task needs
the chance that worker w receives task t through recruitment
the chance that worker w will actually do task t after receiving it
cap the counted value at the task demand so that oversupply is not rewarded

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Worker 1 has reach 0.9 and fit 0.8, so useful contribution is 0.72.
Worker 2 has reach 0.8 and fit 0.7, so useful contribution is 0.56.
Worker 3 has reach 0.7 and fit 0.9, so useful contribution is 0.63.
ETS for Task A is min(2, 1.91) = 1.91, so the plan is still short of full coverage.

math.note: The demand cap is essential because otherwise the planner would keep stacking workers onto one task even after extra recruits stop adding useful work.

charts.title: Recruit by spread only
charts.note: Spread-only planning wastes effort because it cannot tell whether recruited workers match the tasks that still need help.

charts.title: GKD-Recruiter
charts.note: The joint model fills more useful slots because it balances social reach with actual task completion and respects demand limits.

items.html: If worker location or task preference changes quickly, then old fit scores will mislead the planner because the chosen seeds may recruit people who no longer match the work.

items.b: Spread estimates may miss real social behavior.
items.html: If contact links look strong in historical data but workers ignore current requests, then the reach model will overcount future recruitment because past sharing does not always repeat.

items.b: Demand caps make the search uneven.
items.html: A small seed change can suddenly stop paying off when a task becomes full, so local search rules can look unstable because one more recruit may be valuable for one task and worthless for another.
The system works best when worker movement, task demand, and contact behavior are refreshed often, because then the combined scores stay aligned with the real world.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small city map with a few workers, tasks, and social links. Give each worker a location, a set of preferred task types, and a chance of passing tasks to contacts. Then compare three policies: pick seeds by social degree only, pick seeds by task fit only, and pick seeds with the joint objective above.

Track how many task slots are filled and how many extra recruited workers land on already-full tasks. The demo should show that the joint policy wins because it sends recruitment toward people who are both reachable and useful.
demo.closing: A convincing demo must show fewer wasted recruits and more filled task slots, because the paper's main claim is about useful completion rather than raw spread.
